title: Tencent Raises $5.7B for AI Chips in Oversubscribed Bond Sale
summary:
More than $23 billion in orders flowed into Tencent's latest debt offerings to fund the expansion of the company's computing capabilities. The internet giant raised approximately $5.7 billion through a combination of US dollar and offshore yuan bonds, exceeding its own $5 billion target and a $4.5 billion minimum expectation reported by Reuters. To support the raise, the company issued US dollar notes across 10 and 20 year tenors and offshore yuan bonds with 10 and 30 year maturities.

The proceeds are primarily earmarked for AI chip purchases as Tencent accelerates its infrastructure buildout. Spending on AI and computing rose 176% to 52.8 billion yuan in the June quarter, with annual expenditures projected to top 200 billion yuan, or roughly $30 billion. This shift toward utilizing the debt market reflects the extreme capital requirements of the AI race in China, even for the region's most profitable technology firms.

selectedTweets.text:
China's biggest tech companies are now BORROWING money to buy AI chips.

Tencent told bond investors its roughly $5 billion bond deal will mainly fund AI spending, according to Bloomberg. Management said most of that AI spending will go toward chip purchases. The deal includes $1.5 billion to $2 billion in dollar bonds and 20 billion to 25 billion yuan in offshore yuan bonds, and it could be priced as early as today. Tencent's spending on AI and computing already rose 176% to 52.8 billion yuan in the June quarter. At that pace, its spending for the full year would come in a little above 200 billion yuan, or about $30 billion.

To be fair, Tencent has huge cash flow and only one dollar bond due before 2028, so this is not a company in trouble. But here's why it matters because first, AI spending is now so big that even the most profitable companies are turning to debt to pay for it. Second, every dollar Tencent puts into chips is more demand for AI hardware and memory, even with export limits on the best United States chips. Third, it shows the AI race in China is speeding UP, not slowing down.

Anyone calling the top on AI spending should watch what the biggest buyers are doing, not what the stock market did on one bad day.
selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
Just 10 stocks are responsible for 70% of the S&P 500's entire rally since March 30th.

The S&P 500 has gained roughly 23% since its March lows, but the overwhelming majority of those gains have come from just a handful of companies. $NVDA alone accounts for 13% of the rally, followed by $MU, $AAPL, and $MSFT at 9% each, $AMD at 8%, and $GOOG at 7%.

Meanwhile, the other 490 companies in the index collectively contributed just 30% of the gains and if you look closely at the biggest contributors, there's a pretty obvious trend. A HUGE portion of this rally has been driven by companies benefiting directly or indirectly from the AI infrastructure buildout.

This is also why I keep saying that simply looking at the S&P 500 doesn't tell you the entire story of what's happening in the market. The index might be hitting new highs, but that doesn't necessarily mean the average stock is performing anywhere near as well. You could have a market where the S&P 500 is up more than 20%, yet plenty of individual stocks are barely moving or even trading in the red. And that's exactly what happens when the index becomes increasingly dependent on a small number of companies to generate returns.

Personally, I still believe the broader AI infrastructure trade has plenty of room to run, especially as spending on memory, compute, networking, and power continues accelerating. However, this chart also tells us something important about the current market. Investors are becoming increasingly selective about where they're putting their money, and right now, a relatively small group of companies is capturing most of those inflows. As long as these companies continue delivering strong earnings and guidance, I don't see that changing anytime soon.
